articles.title: What to expect at 4th ICC status conference in Rodrigo Duterte's case
articles.summary: PRAGUE, Czechia - The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III will convene the fourth status conference on Tuesday, October 13, to discuss procedural matters before the trial of former…
articles.byline: ANDY PEÑAFUERTE III, JAY-VEE MARASIGAN PANGAN, Reuters

blocks.text: PRAGUE, Czechia – The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III will convene the fourth status conference on Tuesday, October 13, to discuss procedural matters before the trial of former President Rodrigo Duterte on crimes against humanity charges.

Trial Chamber III is scheduled to sit from 10 a.m. to 11:30 am local time (5 p.m. to 6:30 p.m. Manila time), with another block from noon to 1:30 p.m. (7 p.m. to 8:30 p.m. Manila time) if more time is needed.
Will Duterte attend the status conference?
According to the ICC Public Affairs Unit, Duterte is expected to be present at the hearing. This will be his third appearance before the court overall.
How can the public watch the conference?
Yes. The ICC will stream the hearing on its website with a 30-minute delay.
The ICC Public Affairs Unit said it will make available the audiovisual links from the hearing afterward.
What would be the daily sitting schedule during the trial?
At the status conference, the judges are expected to discuss how long the Court should sit for opening statements and the first block of evidence in December 2026.

In its October 8 decision, the Chamber adopted a flexible, case-by-case approach, balancing considerations of Duterte’s health with the needs of witnesses, such as those testifying via video link from the Philippines.
The Registry initially proposed the following reduced sitting hours (in local and Manila time):

These sitting hours, alongside a “bloc” schedule (e.g., sitting for three weeks followed by two weeks off), were recommended by the Registry based on the expert panel’s medical examination of Duterte.
What’s the update on the Prosecution’s List of Witnesses?

Trial Chamber III will ask the prosecutors how many witnesses they plan to call and how many hours they expect to need to present their case. The defense and the Common Legal Representatives of Victims will also give their estimates.
Following a judicial ruling on October 9, the Chamber ordered the Prosecution to update its witness list, evidence list, and Trial Brief by October 16 to reflect the formal exclusion of Incident 57.

The Chamber decided on October 2 that for Rule 68(3) witnesses, the Prosecution’s supplementary examination of witness P-1100 was capped at 1 hour, reducing the Prosecution’s requested 2 hours to avoid defeating the purpose of streamlined Rule 68 testimony.
However, the Chamber rejected four associated items that were not adequately explained or used in the witness's statement.
The Defense is expected to present its response to Rule 68 applications and requests for in-court protective measures.

The Chamber previously warned the Prosecution and Defense to conduct rigorous assessments before filing future Rule 68 applications to avoid over-inundating the record with repetitive or minimally relevant material.
Where are the proceedings at now about the disclosure of evidence?
The judges will return to disclosure and the prosecution’s List of Evidence, including recent filings that have raised disputes over how material was reviewed and turned over to the defense.
Based on the Defense’s September 22 motion, the case record currently sits at 62,130 items (over 320,000 pages), with 19,238 listed on the Prosecution's List of Evidence.

The Defense argued that the record is flooded with untriaged, illegible, or duplicate documents, primarily from a 44,400+ item dataset on what it emphasized as “drug-related deaths”. It has asked the Chamber to order a new case record capped at 10,000 items. A decision on this is pending.
However, the Prosecution countered in its October 5 response that the volume is necessary to establish contextual elements of widespread attacks against civilians.
The Prosecution also revealed it had offered a set of agreed facts that would have removed approximately 42,511 items from the case record, but the Defense rejected the proposal.
The Chamber has yet to decide on the Defense’s October 9 request to respond to the relevance and review of the Prosecution’s dataset.

In response to Defense’s arguments that thousands of documents in Tagalog or Cebuano lack English translations, the Prosecution noted that 1,591 of these items were disclosed under Rule 77/exculpatory obligations, which do not require official court translation. The Prosecution also said approximately 130 are silent video clips (such as CCTV footage), and remaining metadata linking issues are being corrected.
Is the Defense ready for the trial?

The Chamber has specifically included the defense’s readiness for trial on the agenda, giving Duterte’s lawyers an opportunity to explain whether they are prepared for the proceedings and whether outstanding issues still affect their preparations.

At the third status conference, the Defense maintained that proceeding with the November 30 trial start date severely prejudices Duterte, given that nearly 57,000 items were disclosed in the final months before trial.
The Defense emphasized the massive time burden required for trial preparation, estimating that reviewing the 62,130 disclosed items would take roughly 16,000 person-hours.

On September 25, the Defense proposed that the Chamber order the Prosecution to liaise with the Registry to create a case record capped at 10,000 items as a compromise to keep the 30 November trial date feasible.
The Chamber reiterated in its October 2 decision that the Defense retains full discretion over how to use its allocated questioning time during trial.
Meanwhile, the Prosecution maintained that the volume of evidence is “reasonable” and that the trial should commence on November 30 as scheduled.
How about the Victims’ Representatives?
The Common Legal Representative for the Victims (CLRV) stated they do not oppose reasonable health accommodations for Duterte, provided they do not prejudice other participants.
The Victims Participation and Reparations Section also highlighted the “strong interest” of victims and affected Philippine communities in following the trial live.
What will the Registry discuss during the status conference?

The Registry is expected to brief the judges on what support it can provide for the trial process. It will also update the court on interpretation arrangements for the start of the trial, an essential practical issue in proceedings involving parties, witnesses, and participants who may use different languages.

In its October 7 filing, the Registry confirmed it can provide an over-ear noise-canceling headset for hearing/interpretation, nursing staff support during breaks, and mobility/seating assistance in court.

If required, the Registry has also prepared protocols to enable Duterte to appear remotely via video link from the ICC Detention Center, complete with dedicated privileged telephone lines for counsel consultation.
Will the public see Duterte in the courtroom during trial?

The Public Information and Outreach Section (PIOS) recommends that the Chamber regularly provide public explanations if Duterte is authorized to leave the courtroom during hearings to mitigate speculation and public concern in the Philippines.
The Registry has ensured that there is no broadcast of Duterte walking into or out of the courtroom. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Christa Pike discharged from hospital and returned to prison, her lawyers say
articles.summary: The convicted murderer was left in a critical condition after she survived two lethal injections.

blocks.text: US death row inmate Christa Pike has been discharged from hospital following her botched execution at the end of last month, her lawyers have said.
The 50-year-old murderer has been returned to the prison where she has spent the last 30 years, according to a statement from her lawyers on Saturday.
She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison.
Pike survived two lethal injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September, which left her in a critical condition in hospital.
Earlier this week, she regained consciousness and began speaking - stunning experts, medical staff and her lawyers.
"She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances," her lawyers said in their statement.
Pike's case is now in uncharted territory as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.

articles.title: Nobel peace laureate says US sanctions on ICC 'unacceptable'
articles.summary: Navi Pillay says the Trump administrations' sweeping penalties on the international tribunal were "unheard of".

blocks.text: Navi Pillay, the winner of this year's Nobel Peace Prize, has called US sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) "unheard of" and "unacceptable".

The South African former ICC judge was awarded the prize on Friday "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said.

US President Donald Trump expressed his disatisfaction with the pick and hours later the US unveiled sweeping sanctions in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it described as a "rogue" institution.
The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.

Pillay, speaking via video link during an event at the Nobel Peace Center in Oslo on Saturday, said: "There is so much tension and anxiety over the continued existence of international courts, mainly the International Criminal Court in The Hague.
"Most importantly, sanctions have been announced by one country against the judges, just for the judicial orders they issue. This is unheard of, unacceptable."

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier said the sanctions - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.
The US has already sanctioned 17 ICC judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to inhibit its ability to operate financially.

However, the US has provided a six-month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns.
The Trump administration claims that the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty.

It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar".
The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in saying they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions.
Pillay, 85, also served as UN rights chief, taking part in high-profile work considering allegations of human rights violations, including in Rwanda, Myanmar and Gaza.

Her early work included defending anti-apartheid activists in South Africa, and on Friday she became the country's fifth Peace Prize winner - following in the footsteps of Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu.

"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked after receiving the prize, a reference to last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition figure María Corina Machado, deciding to gift her prize to the US president.
Trump called the announcement of Pillay as 2026's winner "disgraceful and embarassing", and an "indelible stain on the country of Norway".
He has long indicated he thought he should have been awarded the prestigious prize, and was nominated by several allies for it last year.

articles.title: Saudi capital airport hit again, sparking evacuations, reports say
articles.summary: The suspected attack comes a day after Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed two deadly attacks on the Riyadh airport.

blocks.text: An international airport in the Saudi capital has been attacked again, reports say, just days after Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed two successful attacks on the hub.
King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was evacuated after a loud blast was heard on Saturday, two international news agencies have reported.

More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing to the airport, according to Reuters, citing an eyewitness. Saudi authorities have not commented, while the airport told passengers to check with their airline before travelling there.
The attack comes a day after authorities said three Saudi nationals, including a pilot, were killed in two attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis the day prior.
Another three people were killed in Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports on 6 and 7 October.
They came during a marked escalation in renewed fighting between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west.
The Houthis say they are targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war.
The conflict worsened after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive.

That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping. Yemeni pro-government forces have since said they had "secured" the strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.
A Saudi-led coalition was formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government.

A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
But the informal truce began to unravel in July.

The Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. They said they were retaliating against what they described as a years-long Saudi blockade and for an air strike on Sanaa airport.

articles.title: Camden council was warned about paedophile nursery worker years before arrest
articles.summary:
Vincent Chan went on to abuse children after being cleared of ‘significant concerns’ following council-overseen inquiry

A paedophile nursery worker was cleared by an investigation overseen…

blocks.text: A paedophile nursery worker was cleared by an investigation overseen by a local authority three years before he was arrested.

In February, Vincent Chan was jailed after pleading guilty to 56 offences, including assault by penetration on three-year-old girls in his care at a Bright Horizons nursery on Finchley Road in north-west London. After his conviction, prosecutors described him as a “prolific sexual predator”.

The Guardian can now reveal that Chan was the subject of an earlier safeguarding investigation, carried out by Bright Horizons, with the oversight of Camden council. It followed what were described as “significant concerns” raised with the nursery in 2021 about Chan’s conduct and behaviour by the parent of a young girl, including concerns about what her daughter was saying to her about Chan.

Bright Horizons referred the matter to Camden council, which advised the nursery to investigate. Chan was put on duties that involved no contact with children while the investigation by Bright Horizons took place. After it was completed, Chan was cleared to return to his role caring for young children in the nursery.
A year later, in 2022, Chan filmed himself sexually abusing three-year-old girls at the Bright Horizons nursery.
Chan was first arrested in June 2024, initially on suspicion of child cruelty, after nursery staff discovered videos Chan had filmed of distressed children in his care.

After Chan’s devices were searched by police as part of this investigation, they discovered that he was a prolific sexual offender, with tens of thousands of child abuse images on his computer. He had also committed sexual offences in his previous job as a teaching assistant at St Mary’s Church of England primary school in Dollis Park, north London, including upskirting female pupils. In February this year, Chan was sentenced to 18 years in prison.

The revelation that Camden council and Bright Horizons were aware of concerns about Chan three years before his arrest, and that there had been an investigation into his behaviour, will raise questions about whether there were earlier opportunities to stop him. It will also raise wider questions about whether existing safeguards for nurseries are adequate.

In early 2024, prior to Chan’s arrest, other parents say that they raised concerns with Bright Horizons about Chan’s conduct at work. They say they warned Bright Horizons that their children were telling them that Chan shouted at them, was “angry” and a “bad man”. These parents say these concerns were dismissed. After Chan’s first arrest, the Bright Horizons nursery on Finchley Road closed in June 2025.

Nurseries have a responsibility to refer to local authority designated officers (LADOs) when there are concerns that a nursery worker has been accused of harming or posing a risk of harm to children, may be guilty of criminal conduct, or has exhibited behaviour that makes them unsuitable to work with children.
Local authorities have the ultimate responsibility for managing allegations raised that relate to adults who work with children.

LADOs can recommend that a matter be referred to the police if they believe it meets a criminal threshold. It is understood that the Metropolitan police did not receive a referral in 2021 regarding Chan, and were only notified of the concerns subsequently.

After Chan’s sexual offending came to light, Camden council carried out a rapid review of the decision to clear him to return to work after the Bright Horizons investigation. The review concluded in November 2025, and Camden council subsequently commissioned a local child safeguarding practice review, led by an independent reviewer, to examine how Chan was able to abuse children at the Finchley Road nursery, in addition to offences committed in his previous role.

The review, which has been pushed back repeatedly, is expected to be published in early 2027 according to Camden council. It is expected to be critical of the safeguarding culture within Bright Horizons. But Camden council has said publicly that it cannot investigate Bright Horizons under health and safety laws because it is conflicted due to its participation in the safeguarding review. Local authorities have the power to prosecute businesses that do not comply with health and safety legislation.

In a letter to the parent of a child at the nursery, seen by the Guardian, Camden council said that the purpose of the safeguarding review was “not conducted to hold individuals, organisations, or agencies to account”. The review is not expected to satisfy the parents of Chan’s victims because it is unlikely to apportion blame to executives at Bright Horizons.

There has been no explanation of why the review was pushed back from summer 2026, when the independent reviewer was initially expected to submit her report. The council has also rejected a freedom of information request from the Guardian relating to Chan’s employment at the nursery, citing a desire to “manage” the release of information.

It is understood that, in addition to the 2021 referral involving Chan, Camden council received other unrelated safeguarding referrals from Bright Horizons between 2017 and 2024, the time Chan worked at the nursery.

A spokesperson for Camden council said: “Children deserve the best care in a safe environment and the ongoing independent local child safeguarding review into this case presents a pivotal opportunity to prevent abuse like this from happening again. Our participation in the review is thorough, and we have disclosed all relevant documents and information.
“We are ready to receive the review’s recommendations once it is published and take action. We are determined to make a real and tangible impact on safeguarding arrangements for the future.”

A spokesperson for Bright Horizons said: “Our thoughts remain with the victims of Chan’s shocking crimes and their families. As the Camden local authority’s child safeguarding practice review is ongoing, we will not be able to comment without the express written authorisation of that committee as we do not wish to prejudice that process. We will respond as soon as we are able, once we have received the committee’s response.”

articles.title: Woman injures three people in third Poland school knife attack in a week
articles.summary: Polish police had already deployed to schools after a female caretaker was killed and several others injured in two earlier attacks in two days.

blocks.text: A woman has been arrested after injuring three people in the third knife attack recorded at schools in Poland this week.
The 21-year-old used a "dangerous object" to attack a 17-year-old girl at an educational institution in the capital Warsaw, police have told news agencies PAP and AP.
It comes a day after thousands of police visited schools across Poland following two stabbing attacks earlier in the week, one of which killed a female caretaker.
A Warsaw police spokesperson said they could not confirm whether the latest incident was related to the two previous attacks.

Authorities told local media that the 17-year-old injured on Saturday had been taken to hospital, but her condition is not life-threatening. Two other women aged 17 and 24, who had come to submit enrolment documents were also injured, the state news agency reported.
Police told local media that the suspected attacker was a student at the school and initial findings suggest she did not know the three victims.

Schools in Poland had been stepping up security following knife attacks at schools across the country on 7 and 8 October. Polish police said they had arrested 76 people after deploying to schools across the country.
"When it comes to the safety of Polish children and peace in our schools, there is no room for compromise," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said ahead of the operation.
Local media, citing a police spokesperson, reported authorities had information to suggest incidents this past week could be related to an internet challenge.
On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student attacked and injured nine people at a vocational school in the central Polish province of Mazovian.
A day later, a 37-year-old caretaker was killed after a 15-year-old entered a primary school in Leszczydół-Nowiny, north of Warsaw.

Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński also said a 17-year-old was detained in the town of Sierpc, north-west of Warsaw, after allegedly stating "on school grounds that he planned to do something... dangerous - that he intended to harm someone".

articles.summary: Davao City Rep. Paolo “Pulong” Duterte questioned why the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) needed his insights if it was confident in the results of the lie detector test administered to former…

blocks.text: Published October 10, 2026 10:54pm

Davao City Rep. Paolo “Pulong” Duterte questioned why the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) needed his insights if it was confident in the lie detector test results administered to former police officer Rodulfo Gracioso Jr.
Earlier on Saturday, the NBI said it invited Duterte to shed light on Gracioso’s controversial claims, including that he delivered bags of cash to the lawmaker and other family members.
In a Facebook post, Duterte questioned the NBI’s decision to seek his side despite its assessment of Gracioso’s credibility.
“99.9% legit si Gracioso base sa lie detector test ng NBI di ba?” Duterte said.
(Gracioso is 99.9% credible based on the NBI’s lie detector test, right?)

“Aba, kung ganoon pala kayo ka-kumpiyansa sa kanya, bakit kailangan pa ang insights ko? Para saan—may kulang pa ba sa ebidensiya, o kulang lang sa kumpiyansa ang NBI sa sarili nilang assessment?” he added.
(If you are so confident in him, why do you still need my insights? What for—is there something lacking in the evidence, or does the NBI lack confidence in its own assessment?)

NBI Director Melvin Matibag had previously said Gracioso’s claims were 99% truthful based on the polygraph test conducted by the agency. Gracioso has taken at least two lie detector tests, according to the NBI.
If Gracioso’s affidavit was 99.9% credible, the case should stand on its own, Duterte said.
“Hindi naman ako ang nagsabi ng 99.9%. Kayo ang nagsabi niyan. So, put your money where your mouth is. Kung hindi, huwag ninyo akong gawing pampalakas ng loob,” Duterte said.
(I am not the one who said 99.9%. You were the ones who said that. So, put your money where your mouth is. Otherwise, do not use me to boost your confidence.)

Gracioso came forward claiming to have served as a bagman for former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco. He alleged that he delivered money to various political personalities, including several contractors implicated in the flood control corruption scandal.
His claims, however, were disputed by Curlee Discaya, one of the private contractors being linked to the flood control fund mess.—MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Same Chinese militia vessel returns to Kota Island after 11 days
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The same Chinese maritime militia vessel has intruded into the waters of Philippine-held Kota Island in the West Philippine Sea for the second time in less than two weeks,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The same Chinese maritime militia vessel has intruded into the waters of Philippine-held Kota Island in the West Philippine Sea for the second time in less than two weeks, prompting authorities to warn against repeated attempts to challenge the country’s sovereignty.

The National Task Force for the West Philippine Sea (NTF-WPS) said on Saturday that Chinese Maritime Militia Vessel 9622 returned to the area on Friday, Oct. 9, accompanied by 22 sampans that engaged in unauthorized fishing and reportedly dumped waste at sea.

During the encounter, the Chinese mothership encircled Philippine patrol boats responding to the intrusion, while its captain claimed the waters as Chinese territory and ordered Filipino personnel to leave, according to the task force.
The same Chinese vessel had deployed 24 sampans near Kota Island on Sept. 28, marking two reported incursions involving the vessel in just 11 days.
“Such repeated incursions underscore the need for sustained vigilance and a clear, consistent response to attempts to challenge Philippine sovereignty,” the NTF-WPS said.
In the latest incident, one of the Chinese sampans approached within 250 meters of Kota Island’s shoreline, according to the task force.

Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) personnel, supported by the Philippine Marine Corps and Philippine Navy, moved to confront the Chinese vessels, prompting the mothership to maneuver around and encircle their boats.
Despite the confrontation, Philippine forces managed to drive all the Chinese vessels out of the island’s territorial waters, the NTF-WPS said.

The task force condemned the latest intrusion, saying the Chinese vessels’ unauthorized fishing activities violated Republic Act No. 12064, or the Philippine Maritime Zones Act, and the Philippine Fisheries Code, as amended by Republic Act No. 10654.

Kota Island, also known as Loaita Island, is part of the Kalayaan Island Group under the municipality of Kalayaan in Palawan. The Philippines occupies and administers the island, although China also claims sovereignty over it.
The NTF-WPS maintained that the island and its territorial sea are under Philippine sovereignty, rejecting China’s territorial claim.
“China’s claim over the area has no basis under international law,” it said.

The latest encounter adds to a series of confrontations between Philippine and Chinese vessels in the West Philippine Sea, where Beijing continues to assert expansive maritime claims despite the 2016 arbitral ruling that rejected its claims to historic rights within the so-called nine-dash line.
The ruling, however, did not determine sovereignty over disputed islands and other land features.
The NTF-WPS commended the PCG, Philippine Marine Corps and Philippine Navy for their coordinated response, which resulted in the departure of the Chinese vessels.
It also warned against allowing repeated Chinese incursions and assertions of sovereignty to become commonplace in Philippine waters.
“Repeated intrusions, coercive maneuvers, and baseless assertions of sovereignty will not be allowed to become normalized in Philippine waters,” the task force said.
The NTF-WPS said the government would continue supporting Philippine maritime and security forces in protecting the country’s territory and maritime rights.

It added that the Philippines would respond to similar incidents “firmly, lawfully, and resolutely” to defend its sovereignty, territorial integrity and national interests in the West Philippine Sea. /mr

Both sides have been accused of using drone attacks.
Ocha said in a statement that the area reportedly struck on Friday had been "under sustained atttack in recent weeks, displacing thousands of civilians and exposing many more to grave harm".

articles.title: Ukraine hit by deadly Russian strikes as ‘thanks’ for Trump diesel deal, Zelenskyy says
articles.summary:
Ukrainian president says money from fuel sales will intensify war as European leaders reiterate support for Kyiv

Russia launched deadly strikes on civilians in Ukraine as “thanks” for a deal…

blocks.text: Russia launched deadly strikes on civilians in Ukraine as “thanks” for a deal cut by Donald Trump with Vladimir Putin to buy large quantities of Russian diesel, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, accusing Washington of helping fund Moscow’s war.

The Ukrainian president has expressed repeated outrage at the agreement announced by Trump on Friday, which the US president said was needed to reduce diesel prices, and comes ahead of November midterm elections where the cost of fuel is a key voter issue.
The deal, which appeared to blindside Kyiv as it was announced while Ukrainian negotiators were in Miami for peace talks, was described by Zelenskyy as a “gift” to Russia’s president.

He said Russia would use the money it raised from the fuel sales to invest in its war and that “any easing of sanctions” would play into Russia’s hands, “allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer”.

That prediction was realised hours later, when Ukrainian officials announced that a barrage of Russian strikes on the country’s south-east early on Saturday had killed 15 people, including three children.

blocks.caption: Rescuers working at the site of an apartment building damaged by a Russian strike in Zaporizhzhia. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: “Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy said on social media on Saturday.

“Last night confirmed once again that in Russia, they take any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed,” he said.
There were also “large-scale power outages” in the capital, Kyiv, the country’s largest private energy provider said.

In stark contrast to Zelenskyy’s open frustration with Trump, a Kremlin readout of Friday’s call between the US president and Putin was glowing, with the Russian ⁠news agency Interfax ⁠quoting ​an aide as saying it was “very substantive and friendly”.

“Neither wanted to be the first to hang up,” the Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said of the two leaders. “They hung up simultaneously, literally at the same time.” ​Zelenskyy has previously said Putin is playing games with Trump.

The diesel deal disrupts four years of western financial pressure on Moscow and leaves Kyiv’s allies in Europe and Nato scrambling to adapt their sanctions plan. The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the diesel deal “provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war”.

“This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won’t,” she said on Saturday. “On Monday, EU foreign ministers intend to approve the biggest set of sanctions listings targeting Russia’s war machine since the start of the war.” She was referring to plans to formally add 1,600 new individuals and entities to the EU’s sanctions blacklist.

blocks.caption: Kaja Kallas with Volodymyr Zelenskyy at a summit in Copenhagen last year. Photograph: Piroschka Van De Wouw/Reuters

blocks.text: Major European governments have attempted to balance their diplomatic and trade relationship with a mercurial Trump and their support for Ukraine.

The German government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said Berlin “remains committed to the sanctions imposed on Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions”, adding that support for Ukraine “remains unwavering”.
Ulf Kristersson, the Swedish prime minister, expressed “regret” at the US agreement, saying energy revenues were “a vital source of funding Russia’s war of aggression”.

Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia “must feel its losses” and has promised to respond. In the Russian-occupied ‌Luhansk ‌region, Ukrainian attacks in the past 24 hours had killed four ⁠civilians and wounded ⁠five, the region’s ‌Russian-installed governor, Leonid Pasechnik, said ​on Saturday.
Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was ready to take “de-escalatory steps” in the war but only if Russia did the same.

articles.title: Isaias weakens to post-tropical cyclone after striking Florida panhandle
articles.summary:
Nearly a million people are without power in Florida, Alabama and Georgia as rain and flooding remain a concern

Isaias weakened on Saturday to a post-tropical cyclone after

blocks.text: Isaias weakened on Saturday to a post-tropical cyclone after striking Florida’s panhandle as a category 2 hurricane the previous night, though it still posed flooding and tornado threats as it moved inland.
More than 868,000 customers were without power across Florida, Alabama and Georgia on early Saturday as those in the path of the storm began the cleanup process, according to PowerOutage.us.

Although storm surge and tropical storm warnings associated with Isaias had been discontinued, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) warned there would still likely be “considerable impacts” associated with Isaias across much of southern Alabama, Florida’s panhandle and south-western Georgia.

“Flash, urban and river flooding is possible across the region,” the NHC said in a Saturday-morning advisory, adding that there was a considerable potential for flash flooding and landslides across the southern Appalachians. “A risk for tornadoes will persist … through [Saturday] afternoon across parts of the eastern Florida panhandle, Georgia and the Carolinas.”

Isaias through Sunday is expected to produce rainfall amounts of 4-8in across southern Alabama, Florida’s panhandle and Big Bend regions, and south-west Georgia. Localized totals up to 15in are possible, particularly within rain bands across the Florida panhandle and Big Bend.

Across much of the remainder of the south-east US, rainfall amounts of 2-5in are expected, and localized higher amounts up to 10in are possible, especially across the southern Appalachians and coastal Carolinas.

Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, on Friday as a potent category 2 hurricane. It was an atypically late-forming first Atlantic hurricane of the season and lashed the US Gulf coast with heavy rain, fierce winds and life-threatening flooding.
The hurricane’s maximum sustained winds were 105mph (169km/h) and it was predicted to dissipate on Sunday.
Alabama’s governor, Kay Ivey, warned of “possible spinoff tornadoes” and asked residents to “prepare for the worst”.

“Right now, we are worried about strong winds, heavy rain and possible spinoff tornadoes in certain parts of the state,” Ivey said. “As we approach the weekend and any travel plans, make sure you have reliable information as conditions develop. We often hear in emergency management: Hope for the best. Prepare for the worst.
“That is the approach we need with this particular storm system.”

Florida’s governor, Ron DeSantis, said in an interview with Fox News on Saturday morning that his administration had not received any reports of fatalities yet in the state. He attributed that to likely heightened preparation and previous experience with other tropical storms and hurricanes.
“We’re a peninsula in the middle of a tropical part of the world,” DeSantis said. “We’ve gotta deal with these things,” DeSantis said.

And while the stronger El Niño seemed to limit the number of hurricanes in the Atlantic for the year so far, Isaias forming in October with maximum sustained winds of 105mph marked a stark contrast from historical trends.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) predicted a quiet year in terms of hurricanes at the beginning of a season that officially begins annually on 1 June. Noaa anticipated between three and six hurricanes, well below the average of seven. An August forecast from Noaa cut the expected number to between two and six.

Isais is one of the two latest-forming Atlantic hurricanes on record, tying a record set on 8 October 1905. Otherwise, the second-latest date for the first Atlantic hurricane was 11 September – in 2002 and 2013.
None of the eight previous named storms of the 2026 Atlantic season intensified above tropical storm status.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: ‘People are leaving’: New York City’s EMS workers are struggling to make ends meet
articles.summary:
EMS workers, who make life-or-death decisions in emergencies, are the lowest paid first responders

After 31 years in New York City’s emergency medical services, Oren Barzilay has started…

blocks.text: After 31 years in New York City’s emergency medical services, Oren Barzilay has started giving young New Yorkers advice he never imagined giving when he began his EMS career. “Don’t come here,” he tells them. “You are only going to hurt yourself.”

It is a striking reversal for Barzilay, the recently retired president of FDNY EMS Local 2507. What changed for Barzilay was not his view of work or the value of service. It was what he believes is the New York City failure to pay the people who put their lives at risk to save the lives of others.
“After 31 years, I am stuck at $59,000,” he said.

Barzilay’s reversal comes as New York City’s EMS workforces remain locked in a years-long fight over wages and pay parity. The fight has become an early test of a contradiction facing Mamdani’s young administration.

As a candidate, Mamdani built his political identity in part around organized labor, affordability and demands that employers pay workers more. As mayor, he now sits on the other side of the bargaining table, responsible for a vast municipal workforce and a finite city budget. EMS workers’ years-long campaign for higher wages and pay parity – unfolding as his administration filed a lawsuit to stop $10,000 payments to public-school paraprofessionals in court – is forcing that tension into the open.

For many EMS workers their job is a passionate calling. Natasha Villaruel, a paramedic, has about 20 seconds to make a life-saving decision. When the 36-year-old paramedic receives a 911 call for someone in respiratory distress, the routine begins almost automatically, with precision. “You respond with lights and sirens safely. You try to get there as fast as you can,” said Villaruel over the phone.
By the time she and her fellow paramedic reach the doorway, she is already reading the patient’s vitals.

“You assess the patient from the door to see how they’re breathing, to see the color of their skin,” she said. “The first thing you want to know is if they can speak, because now if they can’t speak, you know this is very, very urgent.”
Villaruel, who was born in Jamaica and moved to Brooklyn at four, described the pressure of those first few seconds. “Within 20 seconds, you have to make a life decision.”

More than 4,500 EMS workers such as Villaruel respond to over 1.9mmedical and fire emergencies each year across New York City’s five boroughs, making life-or-death decisions for a city of more than 8.58 million people. Yet the workers entrusted with those decisions are among the lowest-paid first responders in the city. An FDNY EMT starts at $39,386 a year, barely above New York City’s minimum wage. After five years, an EMT can earn roughly $59,534, but a firefighter with similar years of experience makes as much as $105,146 – nearly double what EMS and EMTs make. Many EMS workers are struggling to make ends meet.

Villaruel said her own household is sustainable largely because her husband is a firefighter. But her colleagues, she said, have struggled far more. “We have people that live in shelters,” she said. “We have people that get vouchers. We have people that get food stamps.”

Meanwhile, the ambulances are taking longer to reach New Yorkers facing life-threatening emergencies. The average ambulance response time rose from 11 minutes and 21 seconds in fiscal year 2025 to 13 minutes and 9 seconds in fiscal year 2026, according to the Mayor’s Management Report. The delay in emergency response comes as the city’s EMS system struggles to keep workers. According to New York State EMS workforce report, the number of active EMS responders fell 17.5% between 2019 and 2022 statewide. Union leaders said lower wages are driving an exodus of EMS workers.

“We have a tremendous attrition problem. People are leaving,” said Anthony Almojera, an FDNY EMS paramedic lieutenant and vice president of Local 3621. Almojera said he remains frustrated with the city council and successive administrations. “I don’t know why, over the years, many administrations have decided they do not want to value us,” said Almojera

For some patients, those minutes can be life-altering. “Time matters a lot,” said Dr Shreya Kashyap, second-year neurology resident at Mount Sinai. For patients suffering an acute stroke, she said, every delay can increase the risk of permanent damage to brain tissue. “There’s this phrase that’s very popular in neurology education,” Kashyap said. “It’s called ‘time is brain.’”

The pay disparity is hardly new to city hall. Sandy Nurse, a Brooklyn councilmember, who has supported efforts to raise EMS compensation, said: “EMS workers, frontline emergency management workers, make very, very low wages.” In 2024, Nurse co-sponsored bills to establish a Department of Emergency Medical Services as its own standalone organization, ensuring better wages for service workers as well as mental healthcare. Her progressive caucus also has won $1m for an EMS mental health pilot program.

Barzilay argues that the decades-long failure to achieve pay parity is not due to a lack of political support. He places much of the blame on city hall, particularly the offices responsible for negotiating labor contracts and determining what the city can afford.

Nearly four years after the last contract, the Mamdani administration says negotiations are now underway but declined to disclose when bargaining sessions have taken place or where negotiations currently stand.

“Contract negotiations are currently underway with the EMS union, and we remain fully committed to good-faith bargaining at the table,” Kenneth Londono, communications director for the mayor’s office of labor relations, said in a statement. “The Mamdani administration values the vital, life-saving work that our EMS members perform for New Yorkers every single day.”
Londono said the administration hopes to reach a “fair and sustainable outcome” that supports EMS workers while “remaining fair to city taxpayers”.
Barzilay remains skeptical. Asked whether he believed there are good-faith negotiations under the new administration, he said: “No. Not as of yet.”
Almojera was more hopeful and believes the administration is making a good-faith effort to address the problems facing EMS.
“Negotiations haven’t formally commenced,” Almojera said. “We’re just talking. You know, just talking back and forth.”

For Almojera, Mamdani’s appointment of Lillian Bonsignore as fire commissioner was an encouraging sign. Bonsignore spent 31 years in FDNY EMS, beginning as an EMT before becoming a paramedic and eventually chief of EMS operations. “Making her commissioner is acknowledging that the Fire Department is mostly EMS,” Almojera said. “She knows exactly what we do. She’s one of us.”

Villaruel was less optimistic: “I feel like politicians are politicians,” she said. “They tell you what you want to hear. And then when it’s time for the work to be put in, everyone is blind and deaf.”
Bonsignore’s office did not respond to a request for comment.
For Villaruel, who has spent more than a decade in EMS, the work itself is not what is pushing people away.
“It’s not like they don’t like the job,” Villaruel said. “It’s the pay that’s the problem.”
“Who doesn’t like saving people?” she asked.

articles.title: 'Ragebait' is the 2026 German Youth Word of the Year
articles.summary: Already named the 2025 Oxford Word of the Year, "rage bait" has also been widely adopted in German slang.

image.caption: 'Ragebait' has been selected as the 2026 German Youth Word of the YearImage: Udo Herrmann/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: The 2026 Youth Word of the Year, "Ragebait," was announced on Saturday at the Frankfurt Book Fair by publisher PONS Langenscheidt.
The "Jugendwort des Jahres," or German Youth Word of the Year, is an annual campaign that documents the popularity of new slang expressions.
"Ragebait" (in English: rage bait) refers to social media content that is deliberately designed to make people angry, frustrated or morally outraged.

It aims to drive engagement, since the algorithms of platforms like Instagram, TikTok and X reward high-energy interaction. A post that generates a heated debate through angry comments, or that is widely shared due to the emotional reaction it provokes, counts as high engagement, which leads the platforms to push the content to more feeds.
Shortlist also included 'Peak' and 'Crashout'
"Ragebait" was on a shortlist of three words for the 2026 Youth Word of the Year, alongside "Peak" and "Crashout."
All three terms are borrowed from English, demonstrating once again the language's significant influence on German youth culture.
Around one million young people, aged 11 to 20, have voted since August 28 for their favorite term.
"Ragebait" obtained 36.5% of the votes, followed by 33.8% for "Peak" and 29.7% for "Crashout."

"The close result shows that all three terms have a firm place in the vocabulary of generations Z and Alpha," said Artur Raiser, marketing manager at PONS Langenscheidt, in a press statement. "'Ragebait' held a slight lead from the start," but only by a narrow margin throughout the voting period, he added. "It remained an exciting race for us at the publishing house, too, until the very last moment."
Peak crash out
"Crashout" (used by young Germans as "crashout gehen," or "going crash out") originally comes from the English "to crash out," which traditionally means to fall asleep very quickly due to exhaustion.

But in newer internet slang, popularized on gaming and social media platforms, "crashing out" means having an intense emotional breakdown, losing control of one's temper or reacting with sudden, uncontrolled anger or stress. It is often used with a touch of humor, to emphasize that the reaction might be somewhat exaggerated.
As for the other shortlisted word, "Peak," it refers to something that is the absolute best. In German youth slang, it functions like an adjective: "That was peak football" or "that is peak comedy."

PONS Langenscheidt, a publishing company that specializes in language reference works, has been selecting the German Youth Word of the Year since 2008 — originally via a jury, and since 2020 through an online vote. Offensive, racist or discriminatory terms are not permitted. The multi-stage public nomination and voting process for next year's word will start in the summer of 2027.
"Das crazy" was selected last year, while "Aura" was the Youth Word of the Year 2024.
This article was originally written in German.

Germany 'committed' to further Russia sanctions

blocks.caption: Germany has not purchased Russian oil since 2023 [FILE May 2024]Image: Alexander Ryumin/TASS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Germany on Saturday said it would continue pursuing sanctions against Russia over the war in Ukraine, coming a day after US President Donald Trump announced a temporary US sanctions reprieve on Russian diesel.
"The federal ⁠government ⁠has taken note of the US decision relating to Russian diesel deliveries," government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said in a statement.
"The federal government ​remains committed to the decisions on ​sanctions against ‌Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions," the statement added.
Germany's "support for Ukraine in its struggle to defend itself remains unfailing ... Diplomatic efforts for a peaceful solution continue," he added.
After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Moscow has been subject to round after round of sanctions packages led by the US and EU.
Russian crude and other oil products have been subject to EU sanctions since 2023, and Germany has not imported any oil or oil products from Russia since then.
A spokesperson for Economic Affairs Minister Katherina Reiche said Saturday that "Germany stands fully behind the sanctions packages."
"Our supply is diversified in this area; we are independent of Russian oil," the spokesperson said.
Germany remains Ukraine's largest financial backer in Europe. During a visit to Kyiv last weekend, Chancellor Friedrich Merz reiterated Germany's unwavering support for Ukraine.

In what amounts to a major reversal in US policy, Trump on Friday said he would temporarily lift US sanctions to allow Russia to "immediately" supply over 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to US and global markets.

The move comes as diesel prices reach record levels after the war in Iran launched by the US and Israel sent diesel prices skyrocketing around the world. In the US, the high prices are putting political pressure on Trump's Republicans ahead of the midterm elections in November.
However, despite Trump's claims on social media, it remains unclear how much Russian fuel will reach global markets amid domestic fuel shortages as Ukraine continues to target refineries.

articles.title: How a South African billionaire is turning a corner of Somerset into ‘one man’s estate’
articles.summary:
Koos Bekker’s Newt estate encompasses luxury hotels, pubs and high street business, with local concerns including flooding

When South African billionaire Koos Bekker bought an old country…

blocks.text: When South African billionaire Koos Bekker bought an old country estate in a sleepy corner of Somerset to turn it into a luxury hotel, residents thought it was a sign their area was on the up.

Walking through his peaceful manicured gardens, which feature a maze of apple trees twisted into perfect shapes using the espalier method, it’s easy to feel that all is well in this quiet, picturesque pocket of England.
But if you venture beyond the orchards and into the local pubs, where the local cider sets tongues wagging, you’ll hear a very different story.

Bekker has been embroiled in a row with local people over a number of issues ranging from the vast expansion of his estate, the use of pesticides on it and branding deals – described as “brazen” by one local person – which have seen the local train station named after his hotel, the Newt in Somerset.

blocks.caption: Koos Bekker has been buying thousands of acres around Bruton and Castle Cary. Photograph: Dave Benett/Getty Images for The Newt in Somerset & Burberry

blocks.text: The businessman has a net worth of about £3bn and is the chair of Naspers, one of the world’s biggest technology firms. He has been buying thousands of acres around Bruton and Castle Cary – more than 2,700 acres (1,090 hectares), according to Guardian analysis – through his company Emily Estate (UK) Limited, which trades as the Newt.
As well as swathes of the countryside, Bekker has also snapped up high street businesses from a deli to a beauty parlour, as well as pretty former farmhouses and local pubs.

And it is this expansion of Bekker’s influence beyond the boundaries of the Newt – beloved of celebrities such as Charli xcx and Kate Moss – into the heart of the local Somerset villages where tensions have begun to emerge.

Bekker is not the only moneyed arrival in this corner of Somerset. The area boasts famous residents including former chancellor George Osborne, fashion designer Stella McCartney, and broadcaster Mariella Frostrup.

The George pub in the centre of Castle Cary currently serves senior citizens a hot dinner for just £12, but local people do not expect these prices will remain now the Newt has bought the inn: a bag of chocolate buttons in its farm shop costs £11.95, while a bottle of “cyder” grown on the estate is £12.50.

blocks.caption: Bekker acquired Hadspen House in 2013, along with 16 acres of land, and converted it into the luxury hotel. Photograph: Nick Scott/Alamy

blocks.text: Bekker bought the 17th-century manor Hadspen House in 2013, along with 16 acres of land, converting it into the luxury hotel. Last year he acquired Yarlington Lodge, a Grade II-listed Georgian house a mile away, and converted it into a 32-guest property with its own pool, tennis court and cinema room.

He is hardly a silent investor – the sign for the local train station, Castle Cary, now reads “Castle Cary for the Newt”. By the tracks is the new Creamery cafe, which serves afternoon tea in a vintage Pullman carriage at £45 a head.

Hugh Thomas, a food writer from Frome, said the renaming of the station seemed “arrogant and brazen”, adding: “The station does feel somewhat colonised by the Newt regardless, which I find an encroaching thing, given it is supposed to be a public service.”

blocks.caption: Gardens at the Newt. Photograph: Victor Watts/Alamy

blocks.text: Some, though, have welcomed the investment, saying it has cheered up a previously unloved train station and the Bekker family were creating jobs as well as bringing new people to the area to eat in the restaurants and drink in the pubs.

Visitors to the £800-a-night Newt hotel are invited to enjoy being immersed in the nature of deep Somerset. The hotel recently welcomed a cage of endangered red squirrels. But there, too, lay a problem.

The Newt consulted rewilding expert Derek Gow about keeping five red squirrels in a pen. They became extinct in most of England after invasive grey squirrels were introduced from America which carry a virus that causes a disease called squirrelpox, which kills off the reds.

Gow said: “The Newt did talk to me about it; we did have one conversation. I said: ‘It is not going to be viable.’ It is performative – [the squirrels] are in the cage to show guests. That’s it. Keeping five squirrels in a cage does nothing for wildlife. If they do release them, they will just get squirrelpox and die.”

While the Newt has created spectacular gardens around the hotel, including a historically accurate Roman villa, a “four seasons” garden featuring marble water fountains and a treetop walkway, these are not freely accessible to the public. Only hotel guests and those with an £85 annual pass can enter the grounds.

blocks.caption: The grounds of the Newt are only accessible to hotel guests and those buying an £85 annual pass. Photograph: OBNW/Alamy

blocks.text: People living nearby have also been concerned that there has been an increase in flooding since the Newt was built. The hotel has acknowledged this, and has been digging pools to hold any run-off water from the farm and paved areas.

Local people have set up a group to coordinate complaints about the issue. Emma Craigie, a writer who lives nearby, said: “I live in a village below the hill the Newt is on. In our immediate locality there were incidents of flooding which seemed clearly exacerbated by their road building and hardcore use.”

The worst incident was in May 2023, when rain over the Newt caused flash-flooding down the Pitt and Cam valleys, which the local council described as “beyond levels seen in living memory”. The local authority declared an emergency that evening.
Villagers have also set up a petition against the spraying of pesticides on the Newt’s farmland.

The model and actor Gabriella Wilde, who also lives locally, said: “I was surprised and a little disappointed to learn that they are using such harmful chemicals in their farming operations. That is certainly not the image they project to their guests and local fans. Is it really necessary, especially given how many local farms are making great strides in moving away from old school harmful practices, and towards more nature friendly farming?”

blocks.caption: The croquet lawn to the rear of the hotel building. Photograph: Peter Titmuss/Alamy

blocks.text: Farmers have been suspicious that new boreholes drilled by the hotel have dried up sections of the River Brue, the stream that Bruton is named after. The cider-maker Oliver Dowding, the nextdoor neighbour of the hotel, has entered negotiations with the Newt via the Environment Agency over his section of the river, which runs through his land. He said, ironically, that the newts which used to live on his land had disappeared.

Though the Newt boasts that its food is “locally produced”, its farms do not have organic certification. John Sykes, who lives nearby, pointed to the severely trimmed hedges around the estate as well as the sterile lawns.

“Look, there are no berries for the birds here. And what bothers me is the land immediately adjacent to our village used to be an organic farm, now they’ve bought it, and it isn’t any more. They are continuing to buy farmland, and I don’t know when they will stop. I don’t want to live somewhere that’s just one man’s estate,” Sykes said.

A spokesperson for the Newt in Somerset said: “Fundamental to our philosophy is a love of gardens, respect for the land and a determination to share that passion with a broad audience. To ensure best practice, we employ experts across our operations, including agronomists, horticulturists, arborists, conservationists, educationalists, beekeepers, nutritionists, livestock and wildlife specialists, alongside our hospitality teams.

“We are equally committed to our local community, maintaining close relationships with local organisations and proudly employing more than 650 people, who are either from or live within the local area.”
